You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Kwame Mensah was 78 when he came for treatment, a soft-spoken African American librarian who had spent years building a life around order, quiet, and predictability. He had been married for decades, and much of his daily routine still revolved around the public library where he worked part-time, shelving returns, helping patrons find books, and keeping watch over the reading room. The event he returned to again and again had happened several years earlier, during what should have been an ordinary community outing in the city. He had gone into a busy public square on a weekend afternoon, a place crowded with families, vendors, and people lingering in the sun. The explosion came without warning. What remained most fixed in his mind was not only the blast itself but the sudden rupture of ordinary human conduct around him: the screaming, the shoving, the desperate pushing past the injured, the sight of people knocking others aside to save themselves. Even now, when he spoke of it, what struck him most was how quickly the world had become lawless and cruel. He had come to believe that when people stopped behaving decently, catastrophe was always close at hand.

In the immediate aftermath, Kwame found that the memory did not settle into the past. It stayed sharp, almost unnervingly complete. He could describe the angle of the afternoon light, the sound of metal striking pavement, the expressions on strangers’ faces, the smell in the air after the blast. He said the memory did not feel like remembering so much as re-entering. It played in his mind like a film he had not chosen to watch, beginning with an ordinary street scene and ending in confusion and terror. Sometimes there was no warning. A moment in the present would simply give way, and the whole scene would be there again in full detail.

Over time he noticed that certain situations were especially potent. If he saw people behaving badly in public—someone cutting in line at the library desk, an argument breaking out near the computers, a teenager laughing while another patron complained—his chest tightened and his attention narrowed. In those moments he was no longer only seeing discourtesy; he was bracing for something worse, certain that disorder could turn dangerous in an instant. Anniversaries of the attack were particularly hard. As the date approached each year, he became more vigilant and withdrawn, tracking the calendar with dread even when he tried not to. News coverage and public conversations about terrorism or mass violence could also pull him back immediately. At the library, patrons often discussed current events near the periodicals section, and if he overheard certain topics—bombings overseas, domestic attacks, public safety failures—he felt the old scene surge forward before he could prepare himself.

His responses gradually shaped the way he lived. He stopped going with his wife to festivals, shopping centers, and church events when attendance would be high, insisting that crowded places were too much trouble now. He began turning down invitations that might have brought pleasure—a family cookout, a grandchild’s recital, a neighbor’s retirement party—because he had grown wary of anything that might ask him to relax or feel hopeful. He described this less as sadness than as caution; good moments felt precarious, as though letting his guard down would leave him exposed. When family gatherings became lively, he sometimes went quiet and seemed to disappear into himself, drifting into an internal world so completely that his wife would have to repeat his name to bring him back. He knew this happened, and he was embarrassed by it, but he also felt that slipping away mentally was easier than staying present when conversation or atmosphere became too charged.

At work these patterns had become harder to hide. The library had once suited him perfectly, but now even there he was alert to disruptions. If patrons argued, if a group gathered noisily near the entrance, or if someone began discussing a recent attack on the news, he found himself frozen for a moment, the past arriving all at once with cinematic clarity. He had started arranging his shifts to avoid busier hours and spending more time in back rooms away from the public floor. Colleagues noticed that he no longer joined celebratory staff lunches or retirement gatherings, and his wife had grown hurt by how often he declined outings she hoped they would still share in old age.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was tired of how narrow his life had become. The most recent anniversary had been especially difficult after repeated conversations at the library about a terrorist incident in the news. He found himself replaying his own experience for days, unable to keep the images at a distance, and he realized how little of his world remained outside the event’s reach. What frightened him most was not only the memory itself but the sense that any careless remark, any public misbehavior, any crowd could open it again without warning. What he hoped for, carefully and without much flourish, was to be able to stand in the world with his wife, go to work, hear people talk, and not feel that the film might start at any moment.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Demographics: ethnicity mismatch: The vignette describes him as African American, but the reported demographic is African. All other demographics and self-reported symptom items are reflected.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
